title: The fiftieth listener (Kern ch. 17)
hook: even the fiftieth person to hear it passed on, rejoicing, has great merit

segments.voice: Yesterday, the measure of merit: one moment of trust, weighed above ages of effort. Your line: glad news. Did some good news get its full breath? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

A recipe card sits in a kitchen drawer, stained with butter at one corner. The handwriting is an aunt's. She copied it from a neighbor, who copied it from someone nobody in the family ever met. Nobody in that chain was a chef. Each of them simply liked it enough to hand it on, and somewhere along the way a pinch of something got added. Chapter seventeen of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering, follows a chain like that, link by link, and then asks a surprising question about the person at the very end of it. Today: the fiftieth listener.
screen: `A STAINED RECIPE CARD.` → `COPIED, AND COPIED AGAIN.` → `WHO IS AT THE END?`

segments.voice: First, the question. Maitreya asks the Buddha what merit comes to someone who hears this teaching and rejoices in it. The Sanskrit word here is anumodana: rejoicing, being glad along with someone. Not doing anything yet. Just being glad. Second, the chain. The Buddha answers with a story. Someone hears the teaching in an assembly, goes off to a village or a town, and tells it as well as they can remember to a friend or a relative. That person is glad, and tells another. Who tells another. On and on, until it reaches a fiftieth person, who hears it at the far end of all that retelling, perhaps a little blurred, and rejoices too. Third, the comparison. Set beside that fiftieth listener is a great patron, who gives countless beings everything they could want, for many years, and then teaches them until they reach the highest fruits of the path. The sutra agrees that this patron's merit is enormous. And yet, the Buddha says, the gladness of that fiftieth listener is greater, beyond counting. And if that is true of the fiftieth, he adds, how much more of the first. Fourth, the small acts. The chapter keeps going, almost tenderly. Someone who goes to hear the teaching for a little while. Someone who says to a friend, come and listen with me. Someone who moves over and offers part of their seat to a newcomer. Each of these is honored. The picture is of a teaching that doesn't wear thin as it travels hand to hand. The gladness travels with it, and arrives whole.
screen: `MAITREYA ASKS ABOUT REJOICING.` · `A CHAIN OF FIFTY HEARERS.` · `GLADNESS OUTWEIGHS A GREAT GIFT.` · `EVEN SHARING A SEAT.` · then, large: `PASSED ON AND ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: pass on one good thing. Sit and let the breath settle. Name, quietly, one good thing that reached you through someone else: a book, a kindness, a saying, a way of making tea. Trace it back a link or two if you can. Who gave it to you, and who gave it to them? Then think of one person you could hand it to today. Don't rehearse the words. Just see yourself handing it over, and the other person receiving it. Rest there, with the chain one link longer. The bell holds the time.
The fiftieth listener. In the Lotus Sutra, the one at the end of a long chain of telling, whose simple gladness still carries great merit. Today's word.
Your line: passed on and on. Today, pass along one good thing you received from someone else, and say where it came from. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: In schools that honor the Lotus Sutra, people rejoice in hearing it, invite others to listen, and pass its teaching on; the chapter's picture of a chain of glad hearers is read as encouragement to share the teaching, however secondhand.

fork.reveal: the Buddha says even the fiftieth listener's gladness outweighs a great patron's gift; and how much more, he adds, the first hearer's.

original.note: Sanskrit: rejoicing, being glad along with someone; the key word of this chapter.

trapdoor: what you thought: the fiftieth listener is a number in a contest.
what it means: the last person in a long chain of telling, whose gladness still carries great merit.
what a scholar hears: anumodana, rejoicing in someone else's good, is itself counted as merit; the chapter builds a whole parable on it, so that being glad becomes a practice.

notes: Paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884), ch. 17; nothing quoted.

Check 'how much more the first hearer' and the list of small acts: going to hear briefly, inviting a friend, sharing one's seat with a newcomer.
Kern's chapter title translates anumodana as joyful acceptance; confirm the Sanskrit chapter name and the stress in a-noo-MOH-da-na.
